title: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Most Ingenious Algorithm Ever?
beats: Algorithms split into useful (BFS/DFS) vs beautiful (Towers of Hanoi); FFT claimed to be both
FFT underpins wireless, GPS, signal processing
Usual intro needs DFT/frequency domain; instead discovery approach via polynomial multiplication
Multiply two polynomials by distributive property; coefficient list representation; O(d^2)
Can we do better? Look at simplest polynomial, a line: two coefficients or two points
Degree-d polynomial uniquely fixed by d+1 points; 3 points->quadratic, 4->cubic
Proof sketch via system of equations as matrix-vector product; invertibility, proof linked out
Multiply in value rep: 5 points each, pointwise product, recovers correct degree-4 polynomial; O(d)
Grand plan: evaluate, multiply pointwise, convert back; missing magic box is FFT
Naive evaluation at n random points is O(d^2) again, back where we started
Evaluate x^2 at 8 points: which points let one value imply another? +/- pairs (even)
x^3: same trick with sign flip (odd); only 4 evaluations needed
General polynomial split into even and odd parts as functions of x^2, names given after
Subproblems are evaluation again on squared points, n/2 of them; 'smells like recursion'
Big picture of recursive scheme; would give O(n log n)
'Can you spot the issue?' Squared points all positive; recursion breaks
Can next level stay +/- paired? Only with complex numbers
Reverse-engineer n=4: x1=1, need x2^2=-1 so x2=i; points 1,-1,i,-i
Alternate view: solved x^4=1, fourth roots of unity
Degree 5 -> n=8 -> eighth roots; generalize to nth roots, n power of two
Roots of unity on unit circle; omega = e^(2 pi i/n) via Euler
Why it works: roots are +/- paired, squaring gives n/2 roots, holds every level
FFT outline: base case, two recursive calls, combine using omega^j and omega^(j+n/2)
Tricky step; encourages viewer to pause and verify
11 lines of Python-like code; notes non-power-of-two versions are harder
Back to plan: remaining piece is interpolation
Evaluation as matrix-vector product; DFT matrix named; linear algebra skipped
Show inverse DFT matrix: 'what stands out?' Same with omega^-1 and 1/n
Compare FFT vs inverse FFT; one line of code changes
Recap four ingenious ideas; ties back to favorite/beautiful framing

new_moves.name: reframe-in-familiar-context
new_moves.what: Teach a famous algorithm through a different, familiar problem than its canonical one
new_moves.evidence: 1:24-1:51 FFT via polynomial multiplication instead of time/frequency

new_moves.name: magic-box
new_moves.what: Name a missing component as a black box in a plan before building it

new_moves.name: side-by-side-diff

new_moves.what: Write the constraint the recursion needs and solve for the inputs that satisfy it

theory: The video is a chain of 'can we do better?' questions where each answer creates the next failure: faster multiply needs value rep, value rep needs fast evaluation, pairing breaks at depth two, complex numbers repair it. Failure points become the stepping stones, so the learner feels each idea as forced, not handed down. Roots of unity are derived as the answer to a constraint before they are named.
velocity: Orchestrator: model lessons as a plan with explicit 'magic box' slots filled one by one, revisiting the plan diagram each time a slot is filled
Scene builder: stage a deliberate break (recursion fails on squared points) as its own beat with an inline 'spot the issue' pause
Learner model: delay symbols like omega until learner has computed 1,-1,i,-i by hand; gate notation on completion of the concrete case
Ghost hands: animate code diffs side by side to land 'only one line changed' punchlines
Evals: check that each new tool has a stated reason (why complex, why power of two) before use
